html:
The succession to Muhammad was the dispute over who should lead the Muslim community after the prophet Muhammad died in Medina in 632. It is the origin of the split between Sunni and Shia Muslims.

Muhammad left no clear, agreed instruction. While Ali and the family prepared his burial, a group of leading men of Medina met at a hall called the Saqifa. After debate between the Medinan helpers and the migrants from Mecca, they chose Abu Bakr, one of Muhammad's oldest companions and the father of his wife Aisha, as the first caliph, or successor.

Ali's supporters held that Muhammad had named Ali at Ghadir Khumm and that the choice was wrong. Ali did not make an open fight of it, and the community held together. Abu Bakr was followed by Umar and Uthman, and Ali became the fourth caliph only in 656.

Sunni Muslims honour the first four as the rightly guided caliphs. The Shia hold that Ali should have come first. See Shia Islam and Sunni Islam.
